title: Stephen Kleene and the 1951 Origin of "Regular Expressions"
explainer: In 1951, mathematician Stephen Kleene, trying to formally describe the behavior of simple neuron-like 'nerve net' machines, defined an algebra of 'regular events' using three operations — union, concatenation, and repetition (the 'Kleene star') — that could describe any pattern a finite automaton could recognize. Ken Thompson later built Kleene's notation into the Unix text editor QED and then into ed, the direct ancestor of grep, sed, and every regex engine a security script uses today to parse logs or scan output. The math behind regex is nearly two decades older than Unix itself — scripting just inherited it.

title: The Hacker Ethic's Roots at MIT's Tech Model Railroad Club (late 1950s)
explainer: Journalist Steven Levy's 1984 book Hackers traces the word 'hacker' and its ethic — hands-on curiosity, sharing what you learn, distrust of unnecessary restrictions — to a small group of MIT students in the Tech Model Railroad Club's Signals and Power Subcommittee in the late 1950s, who applied the term to clever, informal fixes to the club's switching system long before it had anything to do with computer security. That same instinct — writing a quick, improvised script to probe or automate something rather than waiting for an official tool — is the direct cultural ancestor of building your own security tooling instead of relying only on packaged software. It's worth knowing the term predates malicious intrusion by decades and originally meant close to the opposite of 'criminal.'
